text: Gang Chen, born in China and known in Chinese as 陈刚 (pinyin: Chén Gāng), is a Chinese-born American mechanical engineer and nanotechnologist. At the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), he holds the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor of Power Engineering position and served as head of the Department of Mechanical Engineering from July 2013 to June 2018. He directs the Solid-State Solar-Thermal Energy Conversion Center, an energy frontier research center previously funded by the United States Department of Energy. Chen was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 2010 and to the National Academy of Sciences in 2023. He earned a Bachelor of Engineering in 1984 and a Master of Engineering in 1987, both in power engineering, from the Huazhong University of Science and Technology, and a Doctor of Philosophy in mechanical engineering from the University of California, Berkeley in 1993. He worked as an assistant professor at Duke University from 1993 to 1997 and as a tenured associate professor at the University of California, Los Angeles from 1996 to 2001 before joining MIT in 2001. Chen has made significant contributions to thermoelectricity, nanotechnology, and thermal engineering. In 2022, he and colleagues discovered that cubic boron arsenide is a highly effective semiconductor with potential applications in electronics. He has received the K.C. Wong Education Foundation fellowship and the John Simon Guggenheim Foundation fellowship (2002–2003), the NSF Young Investigator Award, an R&D 100 award (2008), and the ASME Heat Transfer Memorial Award (2008). He is a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Physical Society, and the American Society of Mechanical Engineers. In 2010, he was elected to the National Academy of Engineering for contributions to heat transfer at the nanoscale and thermoelectric energy conversion technology; in 2014, he was elected an academician of Academia Sinica in the Division of Engineering Science and received the Nukiyama Memorial Award of the Heat Transfer Society of Japan. He was elected a Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in April 2018 and of the National Academy of Sciences in 2023. On January 14, 2021, Chen was arrested by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and charged under the now-abolished China Initiative for allegedly failing to disclose connections to several Chinese educational programs in a U.S. Department of Energy grant application and for omissions in IRS filings, including allegations of wire fraud, failure to file a foreign bank account report (FBAR), and false statements on tax returns. The wire fraud charge stemmed from alleged omissions in an electronically submitted federal grant proposal form (Current and pending support). The FBI documents alleged that Chen received $19 million from China's Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech). In response, MIT President L. Rafael Reif stated the news was "surprising, deeply distressing and hard to understand," and on January 21, 2021, over 100 MIT faculty signed a letter protesting Chen's arrest, citing "deeply flawed and misleading statements" and ending with "we are all Gang Chen," which was shared on Twitter. On January 22, 2021, MIT's president clarified that the funds went to MIT, not Chen, to support a departmental research collaboration with SUSTech that Chen directed on MIT's behalf. The charges provoked widespread criticism, with many MIT faculty joining the protest, stating the defense of Chen was the defense of the scientific enterprise. Bloomberg noted that U.S. science has historically flourished by attracting international talent, and an MIT researcher stated the Department of Justice's China Initiative fundamentally misunderstands research and international collaboration. On January 14, 2022, the Wall Street Journal reported that federal prosecutors recommended dropping the charges, and the Washington Post reported that the DOE forms did not require Chen to disclose his connections to Chinese educational programs, undermining the basis of the charges. On January 20, 2022, federal prosecutors filed a motion to dismiss the charges "in the interests of justice," and the U.S. District Court dismissed the case. In a New York Times interview after his exoneration, Chen described the experience as "traumatic and deeply disillusioning" and stated, "I didn't do anything wrong." After the charges were filed, he was banned from the MIT campus and from contacting MIT employees, and his postdocs were moved to other labs. He lost his research group and funding and worked alone on other topics until the charges were dropped, after which he returned to his MIT office the day following the dismissal of the case.
